requirements.requirement: Existing data under /srv/inventory owned by inventorysvc
requirements.summary: Baseline showed root:root ownership (cmd-c9a53798259140cc). Executor created inventorysvc user and chowned recursively; verification showed inventorysvc:inventory-readers ownership on directory, subdirectory, and both files (cmd-fa3ea50ac6b34a07), confirmed again post-restart (cmd-60386605942845d9).

inventory-readers group created and set as group owner; directories set to 750 (rwx r-x ---) and files to 640 (rw- r-- ---), giving group read/traverse access. inventorysvc (a member of inventory-readers) successfully read file contents both before and after restart.

With directories at 750 and files at 640, no permission bits are granted to others. Explicit test as unrelated user 'nobody' showed both file read and directory listing denied with 'Permission denied', confirmed again after restart.

Baseline showed records.csv and config.json with original sizes/content per prepare baseline hashes. Post-chown verification showed records.csv content unchanged ('sku-1001,keyboard,12\nsku-1002,display,7'), and post-restart verification showed both records.csv and config.json content intact and readable, matching original data with no re-creation or truncation observed.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task — ownership by inventorysvc, group-read access via inventory-readers, exclusion of other users, and preservation of existing file contents — are directly demonstrated with before/after evidence, including explicit positive (inventorysvc read) and negative (nobody denied) access tests. The executor additionally ran the mandated node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart boot id and healthy baseline were captured, a reboot was acknowledged and executed, the post-restart boot id differed, and ownership, permissions, data content, and access control were all re-verified as intact after the restart, consistent with the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is good, with only a trivial leftover log file from the reboot process.
limitations: The reboot log file /tmp/reboot.log was left on the node; while low-risk, it was not cleaned up.

Content preservation was verified by visual comparison of readable text/JSON output rather than a repeated cryptographic hash comparison against the prepare-stage sha256 baseline, though the content shown matches the original data exactly.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace shows a coherent, minimal set of state-changing actions: creating the required group/user, one recursive chown, one recursive chmod pass for dirs and files, and the mandated single reboot (cmd-fa3ea50ac6b34a07, cmd-ac8f3aec47ef4366). All are directly tied to satisfying the task or the mandatory restart-evidence protocol. The reboot left a small residual file /tmp/reboot.log (visible in after_executor temporary-files snapshot, absent in after_prepare), a low-risk, non-sensitive artifact from redirecting reboot command output; it was not cleaned up but poses negligible risk. No failed services, no damaged package state (package-health unchanged 'U var/lib/chrony/chrony.drift' both before and after), and no unnecessary or exploratory mutations were found in the timeline. The 12 failed/timeout commands during the reboot window (cmd-e5fbb1106b2f4d5c through cmd-03c49ecc6a8f415b) are read-only polling attempts during expected node unavailability, not mutations.
